title: A/B Testing and the Two-Party Trap
intro: A/B testing only tells you which version won — not why. Most teams run weak tests with vague hypotheses, then treat the winner as proof. This article covers what makes a test worth running.

learn.title: Weak vs. strong A/B tests
learn.text:
Most A/B tests are weak. They test vague ideas ("we think this version will perform better") with no link to a user problem.

A **strong** test starts with a specific hypothesis: what user behavior are you trying to change, what causes it, and what exactly is changing in the design.

**Weak:** "Make the button brighter because we think it converts better."
**Strong:** "Users miss the primary action because it blends with surrounding content. Increasing contrast and adding a verb label should raise task completion."

right.label: Strong Test
items: Specific hypothesis tied to user problem

try.q: A PM says: "Let's A/B test the new checkout — we changed the layout, copy, and color scheme all at once." What's the problem?
options: You can't attribute the result to any single change
A/B tests need at least 3 variants
Color changes don't affect conversion
You should only test on mobile
try.explain: When multiple things change at once, a win tells you the package won — not which change drove it. You need multivariate testing or staged tests.

learn.title: Match the test to the claim
learn.text:
The size of your claim should match the scope of your test.

→ Changed **one element** (e.g., button label)? You can claim something about that element.
→ Tested a **full redesign**? You can only compare two design packages — not claim any single change drove the result.
→ Changed **several variables**? You need a multivariate test or a staged rollout.

A bigger button getting more clicks could mean: better discoverability, clearer copy, attention pulled from other content, or pressure to act before understanding. Each explanation points to a different fix.

try.q: Your A/B test compared a full page redesign against the original. The new version won. What can you claim?
options: The new design package performed better overall on the measured metric
Every individual change in the redesign was an improvement
The new layout caused the improvement
The old design was bad
try.explain: A full redesign test only compares two packages. You can't attribute the win to any single element — it could be the layout, the copy, or something else entirely.

learn.title: Ground your variations in research
learn.text:
The best A/B tests don't start in a design tool — they start in research.

**Before designing a variation:**
→ Run a usability test to find where users actually struggle
→ Check behavioral analytics and session replays
→ Interview users to understand the problem

**Torres's alternative:** Instead of A/B testing whole ideas, identify your riskiest assumptions and test those individually. A 10-person simulation test on one assumption takes a day. An A/B test on the whole idea takes weeks and still can't tell you which assumption was wrong.

**Before launching a test:**
→ Quick usability check on both variants
→ Define guardrail metrics (support contacts, downstream completion, accessibility)
→ Ask: "What will we learn either way?"

If a test only teaches you something when it wins, it's a weak test. A good test generates insight regardless of outcome.

left.label: Don't
items: Ship the winner without asking why

right.label: Do
items: Ask what you'll learn either way

try.q: Your A/B test shows Variant B raised CTA clicks by 11%. What should you do next?
options: Investigate what else changed that week and who clicked
Ship Variant B immediately
Run the test again with more users
Celebrate and move to the next feature
try.explain: A click increase alone doesn't tell you why. You need to check what else changed, who the clickers were, and what happened after the click.

test.q: What makes an A/B test hypothesis "weak"?
options: It has no link to a specific user problem or expected behavior change
It tests only one variable at a time
It includes guardrail metrics
It runs for too long
test.explain: A weak hypothesis is vague — "we think this will perform better" — with no connection to a user problem or behavioral expectation.

test.q: You A/B test a full page redesign and the new version wins. What can you claim?
options: The new package performed better on the chosen metric
Each individual change was an improvement
The new layout was the key driver
The original design was fundamentally flawed
test.explain: A full redesign test compares two packages. You can't attribute the win to any single change within the redesign.

test.q: What is a guardrail metric in A/B testing?
options: A metric that catches harm outside the primary metric being tested
The minimum sample size needed
The p-value threshold for significance
The baseline conversion rate
test.explain: Guardrail metrics (like support contacts or downstream completion) catch negative effects the primary metric might miss — e.g., clicks went up but confusion increased.

test.q: What's the UX researcher's primary role in A/B testing?
options: Clarify the user problem and turn vague ideas into testable hypotheses
Choose the sample size and run the statistical analysis
Design both variants in Figma
Present the winning variant to stakeholders
test.explain: UXR's role is to ground the test in real user problems, sharpen the hypothesis, flag when too many things change at once, and keep interpretation honest.

test.q: A bigger, brighter CTA button gets more clicks in an A/B test. Which explanation is NOT a plausible cause?
options: The button color scientifically triggers purchasing behavior
The button was easier to discover due to higher contrast
The copy was clearer and more action-oriented
The button pulled attention from surrounding content
test.explain: There's no scientific evidence that specific button colors trigger purchasing. The other explanations — discoverability, clarity, and attention redistribution — are all plausible.
